Who among these four was born earliest?
Zhuge Liang (born 181) is the earliest of the four. After helping found Shu Han, Zhuge Liang exercised near-total authority over both civil and military affairs.
Which of these four is the oldest?
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is an astronomer?
Jabir ibn Hayyan is an astronomer. The c. 215 treatises that survive today mainly deal with alchemy and chemistry, magic, and Shi'ite religious philosophy.

Rhodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rh and atomic number 45.
What is the atomic number of Argon?
Argon is a chemical element; it has symbol Ar and atomic number 18.
In what year was Alan Turing born?
Alan Turing: Alan Mathison Turing (23 June 1912 – 7 June 1954) was an English mathematician, computer scientist, logician, cryptanalyst, philosopher and theoretical biologist.
In what year was Scurvy discovered?
Scurvy or scorbutus is a deficiency disease (state of malnutrition) resulting from a lack of vitamin C (ascorbic acid).
In what year was Polonium discovered?
Polonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Po and atomic number 84.

In which country is Gaboon viper?
Gaboon viper: Gabon. It is the largest member of the genus Bitis.
Who is credited with discovering Radon?
Radon: Friedrich Ernst Dorn. Radon is a chemical element; it has symbol Rn and atomic number 86.
Who is credited with discovering Tautavel Man?
Tautavel Man: Henry de Lumley. Tautavel Man refers to the archaic humans which—from approximately 550,000 to 400,000 years ago—inhabited the Caune de l’Arago, a limestone cave in Tautavel, France.
Who is credited with discovering MDMA?
MDMA: Anton Köllisch. MDMA was first synthesized in 1912 by Merck chemist Anton Köllisch.

A central nervous system stimulant of the phenethylamine class, this combo medication is approved for narcolepsy and ADHD — but is also taken as an appetite suppressant and cognitive enhancer. What is it?
Adderall is the brand name of a fixed-dose combination medication used for the treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy.
These organic compounds, formed when one or more hydrogens in ammonia are replaced by carbon-based groups, are defined by their carbon-nitrogen bonds — what's this class of compounds called?
Amine (UK also) are organic compounds that contain carbon-nitrogen bonds.
This Portuguese economist-turned-dictator ruled as head of government from 1932 to 1968, rebranding his authoritarian regime as the corporatist 'New State.' Who is he?
António de Oliveira Salazar (28 April 1889 - 27 July 1970) was a Portuguese dictator, academic, and economist who served as President of the Council of Ministers of Portugal from 1932 to 1968.
Part of the family Ericaceae, these shrubs flower in April and May in the Northern Hemisphere and October and November south of the equator — what are they called?
Azalea (-) are flowering shrubs in the genus Rhododendron, particularly the former subgenera Tsutsusi (evergreen) and Pentanthera (deciduous).

This scientific discipline, a hybrid of chemistry and biology, studies the chemical processes occurring within living organisms and is generally divided into structural biology, enzymology, and metabolism — what's the field called?
Biochemistry (distinct from chemical biology), is the study of chemical processes within and relating to living organisms.
Present in both sexes from the same embryonic tissue, these two prominences on the upper torso permanently enlarge only in human females at puberty, driven by estrogen and growth hormone - name them?
Breast are two prominences located on the upper ventral region of the torso in humans and other primates.
Indigenous to Asia, this genus of flowering plants includes species like sativa, indica, and ruderalis, and is also commonly known as hemp when grown for non-drug purposes — name the genus?
Cannabis is a genus of flowering plants in the family Cannabaceae that is widely accepted as being indigenous to and originating from the continent of Asia.

The only living member of its genus, this big cat sprints at up to 104 km/h thanks to powerful hindlimbs, long legs, and a flexible spine, and wears black tear-like streaks down its face; which animal is it?
Cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) is a species of large feline and the only living member of the genus Acinonyx.
Mostly belonging to the genus Naja, these venomous snakes are known for rearing upward and flaring a distinctive hood when threatened — name this common snake type?
Cobra is the common name of various venomous snakes, most of which belong to the genus Naja.
Tolerant of poor, sandy soil, this legume was domesticated in Africa millennia ago and is now grown far more in Nigeria and Niger than anywhere else on Earth — which crop?
Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) is an annual herbaceous legume from the genus Vigna.

This common cough suppressant found in cold medicine was combined with bupropion in 2022 to create a fast-acting antidepressant, despite belonging to the same chemical class as morphine — what drug is it?
Dextromethorphan is a cough suppressant used in many cough and cold medicines.
Long used in traditional Indigenous medicine, this prairie-dwelling genus of purple daisy relatives gets its name from a Greek word meaning 'hedgehog' — what plant is it?
Echinacea is a genus of herbaceous flowering plants in the daisy family.

A German Jew who fled the Nazi regime for the United States, this social psychologist and psychoanalyst co-founded a New York psychiatric institute and was associated with the Frankfurt School of critical theory — who is he?
Erich Fromm (March 23, 1900 - March 18, 1980) was a German-American social psychologist, psychoanalyst, sociologist, humanistic philosopher, and democratic socialist.

Native to the Indian subcontinent and Indochina, this fig species carries deep religious significance across four faiths that originated there, including reverence from Hindu and Jain ascetics — what species is it?
Ficus religiosa is a species of fig native to the Indian subcontinent and Indochina that belongs to Moraceae, the fig or mulberry family.
Sometimes mistakenly called the 'stomach flu' even though it's unrelated to influenza, this inflammation of the gut is usually viral, with rotavirus the top cause in children. What condition is it?
Gastroenteritis is an inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract including the stomach and intestine.
Bred for centuries to hunt by sight and speed rather than scent, this ancient dog breed's deep chest, flexible spine, and long legs make it one of the fastest breeds alive. Name the breed?
Greyhound is a breed of dog and a sighthound. It is an ancient breed historically developed for hunting game by sight and speed, and has later been used in organised coursing and greyhound racing.

This field of study concerns the methodological principles of interpretation — especially of biblical, philosophical, and wisdom texts — and has been broadly applied across law, history, and theology — what's it called?

Hermeneutics is the study of the methodological principles of interpretation, especially the interpretation of biblical texts, wisdom literature, and philosophical texts. As necessary, hermeneutics may include the art of understanding and communication.
Defined by Whipple's triad, this condition occurs when blood sugar falls below about 70 mg/dL, causing symptoms like headache, shakiness, confusion, and a fast heart rate — what's it called?

Hypoglycemia (American English), also spelled hypoglycaemia or hypoglycmia (British English), sometimes called low blood sugar, is a fall in blood sugar to levels below normal, typically below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L).
Known for the mantra 'Dying is not a crime,' this euthanasia advocate served eight years in prison after his fourth trial ended in a murder conviction — who is he?
Jack Kevorkian (May 26, 1928 - June 3, 2011), also known by the nickname "Dr.
This 19th-century French mathematician ranged across number theory, complex analysis, and mathematical physics — and his name now sits on a crater on the Moon. Who was he?

Joseph Liouville (24 March 1809 - 8 September 1882) was a French mathematician who worked on a number of different fields in mathematics, including number theory, complex analysis, and mathematical physics.
This inflammation of the voice box causes symptoms ranging from a hoarse voice to complete voice loss, usually clearing up within two weeks. Name the condition?
Laryngitis is inflammation of the larynx (voice box). The primary symptom is loss of some vocal function, ranging from hoarse voice to no voice at all.
Only about 35 atoms of this synthetic element (symbol Lv, number 116) had ever been made as of 2020 — named for a California national laboratory. Which element is it?
Livermorium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lv and atomic number 116.
Sometimes nicknamed 'sea cows,' these large, fully aquatic herbivorous marine mammals can grow up to 13 feet long and include Amazonian, West Indian, and West African species — what are they called?
Manatee (family Trichechidae, genus Trichechus) are large, fully aquatic, mostly herbivorous marine mammals sometimes known as sea cows.
Its three main jobs are converting food into usable energy, building macromolecules like proteins and lipids, and excreting waste — the chemistry that keeps every living thing alive. What is it?
Metabolism (from) refers to the set of life-sustaining chemical reactions that occur within living organisms.
This fast-growing, drought-resistant tree native to northern India earns nicknames like 'drumstick tree' and 'horseradish tree,' and its leaves and seed pods are eaten as vegetables. What is it?
Moringa oleifera is a short-lived, fast-growing, drought-resistant tree of the family Moringaceae, native to northern India and used extensively in South and Southeast Asia.

Encompassing three distinct genetic conditions marked by nervous-system tumors, one type brings café au lait skin spots and scoliosis while another causes early-onset hearing loss and cataracts — which condition?
Neurofibromatosis (NF) refers to a group of three distinct genetic conditions in which tumors grow in the nervous system.
In this learning process, voluntary behaviors grow more frequent through reinforcement or fade through punishment and extinction — what is it called?
Operant conditioning is a learning process in which voluntary behaviors are modified by association with the addition (or removal) of reward or aversive stimuli.
A physician in this medical field — devoted to the study of disease and diagnosing it largely by analyzing tissue and cell samples — is called a pathologist. What is the field?
Pathology is the study of disease. The word pathology also refers to the study of disease in general, incorporating a wide range of biology research fields and medical practices.
This branch of linguistics is concerned with how speech sounds are physically produced, transmitted as sound waves, and perceived by listeners — name the field?
Phonetics is a branch of linguistics that mainly concerns the articulation, sound wave properties, and perception of speech sounds.
Born Joseph Ratzinger in Bavaria, this pontiff led the Catholic Church from 2005 until an unusual resignation in 2013, after which he adopted an 'emeritus' title — who was he?
Pope Benedict XVI (born Joseph Alois Ratzinger; 16 April 1927 - 31 December 2022) was the head of the Catholic Church and sovereign of Vatican City from 2005 until his resignation in 2013.
Like a cosmic lighthouse, this highly magnetized, rapidly rotating neutron star is only visible from Earth when its beam of radiation sweeps directly toward us — what's the object?
Pulsar (pulsating star, on the model of quasar) is a highly magnetized rotating neutron star that emits beams of electromagnetic radiation out of its magnetic poles.

One of the rarest and most valuable precious metals, this hard, corrosion-resistant transition metal with only one naturally occurring isotope is prized for enhancing jewelry — what's the element (symbol Rh, atomic number 45)?
Rhodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rh and atomic number 45.
Also known as Besnier-Boeck-Schaumann disease, this non-infectious condition causes inflammatory cell clusters called granulomata, most often striking the lungs, skin, or lymph nodes — what is it?
Sarcoidosis is a non-infectious granulomatous disease involving abnormal collections of inflammatory cells that form lumps known as granulomata.

This medical state of insufficient blood flow to body tissues comes in four main types, from hypovolemic to cardiogenic, and can progress from weakness and rapid breathing to confusion or cardiac arrest. What is this condition called?
Shock (circulatory) is the state of insufficient blood flow to the tissues of the body as a result of problems with the circulatory system.

Native to China and Vietnam, this invasive planthopper species has spread destructively across the US, feasting on grapevines and stone fruit as well as its preferred invasive host tree — what insect is it?
Spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula) is a species of planthopper indigenous to parts of China and Vietnam.
This West African berry contains a molecule that binds so powerfully to taste buds that sour foods eaten afterward taste sweet instead — what's this plant's common nickname?
Synsepalum dulcificum is a plant in the Sapotaceae family, native to tropical Africa.

When a piece of this obstruction breaks free and travels through the body it's called an embolus, and it can trigger a stroke or heart attack — what is the formation of a blood clot inside a vessel called?
Thrombosis (from Ancient Greek (thrmbsis) 'clotting') is the formation of a blood clot inside a blood vessel, obstructing the flow of blood through the circulatory system.
The most widespread New World scavenger of its kind, this bird sniffs out the gases of early decay to find carrion and rides thermals instead of flapping — which bird?
Turkey vulture (Cathartes aura) is the most widespread of the New World vultures.
This pungent Japanese condiment, ground from the rhizome of a plant related to horseradish and mustard, traditionally accompanies sushi. What is it?

First identified in 1789 and not manufactured at scale until the 1920s, this corrosion-resistant, silvery-grey metal resembles hafnium and takes its name from the mineral that remains its main source — what element, symbol Zr, is it?
Zirconium is a chemical element; it has symbol Zr and atomic number 40.
Produced by oxidizing adrenaline and named for its deep violet color, this compound was studied in the mid-20th century as a possible cause of schizophrenia — what is it?
Adrenochrome: Chemical compound. It was the subject of limited research from the 1950s through to the 1970s as a potential cause of schizophrenia.
This Austrian psychotherapist broke from Freud's circle to found 'individual psychology,' emphasizing birth order and coining the term 'inferiority complex' — who was he?
Named after a French physicist considered a father of electromagnetism, this SI base unit measures electric current and equals one coulomb per second — which unit?
Ampere: SI base unit of electric current. The ampere (symbol: A), often shortened to amp, is the unit of electric current in the International System of Units (SI).
This Soviet single-engine biplane, in production from 1947 to 2001, doubles as a crop-duster, water bomber, and paratroop transport thanks to its rugged, adaptable airframe — what is it?
Antonov An-2: Soviet single-engine civilian aircraft.
Also called the yellow-legged predatory wasp, this insect — native to parts of Southeast Asia — has become an invasive concern across much of Europe — which species?
Asian hornet: Species of insect. The Asian hornet (Vespa velutina), also known as the yellow-legged hornet or Asian predatory wasp, is a species of hornet indigenous to Southeast Asia.
Instead of teeth, these marine mammals sieve plankton through whalebone plates in their mouths — a group of 16 species that includes the rorquals and the bowhead. What do we call them?
According to scholar John Carter, this discipline has two senses: a list of works consulted by an author, and the systematic study of books as physical objects — what's it called?
Bibliography: Organized listing of books and the systematic description of them as objects.

A four-engined American heavy bomber from the 1930s, it dropped more tonnage than any other aircraft in World War II and ranks as the third-most produced bomber in history, after the B-24 and German Ju 88—what is this legendary aircraft?

Boeing B-17 Flying Fortress: American heavy bomber aircraft. The Boeing B-17 Flying Fortress is an American four-engined heavy bomber aircraft that was developed in the mid-1930s for the United States Army Air Corps (USAAC).
Also known as undulant fever or Malta fever, this disease is usually caught by drinking unpasteurized milk from infected animals and tends to persist for life — what is it?
Present in the gut or mouth of up to 60 percent of healthy adults, this opportunistic yeast turns dangerous in immunocompromised patients, causing a common fungal infection — what species is it?
Candida albicans: Species of fungus. Candida albicans is an opportunistic pathogenic yeast that is a common member of the human gut flora.
Named after a Louisiana parish and named the state's official canine in 1979, this herding breed was traditionally used to hunt feral boars — what breed is it?
Catahoula Leopard Dog: American breed of dog.
Known as lamb's quarters, goosefoot, or fat-hen, this fast-growing annual weed in the amaranth family is sometimes cultivated as food elsewhere — which plant?
Chenopodium album: Species of flowering plant in the goosefoot family.
This lincosamide antibiotic treats infections from strep throat to acne, but raises the risk of a specific gut infection roughly fourfold — what is it?
Clindamycin: Antibiotic. It can also be used to treat acne, and some cases of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).
Its species name honors Colchis, an ancient region on the Black Sea, and it's often released into the wild as a game bird — which Asian-native, ring-necked bird is this?
Common pheasant: Species of bird. The common pheasant (Phasianus colchicus), ring-necked pheasant, or blue-headed pheasant, is a bird in the pheasant family (Phasianidae).

Ancient Greek, Chinese, and Indian cultures lacked a concept for this, seeing art as discovery rather than invention, while the Judeo-Christian-Islamic tradition later reserved it for God alone — what mental faculty is this?
Creativity: Forming something new and somehow valuable.
Also known as jimsonweed or devil's trumpet, this poisonous nightshade plant likely native to Central America has been used both in folk medicine and, unpleasantly, as a hallucinogen — which plant?
Datura stramonium: Species of flowering plant in the nightshade family.
Nicknamed the 'businessman's trip' in the 1960s for its rapid onset and short duration, which naturally occurring tryptamine hallucinogen has long been used as a ritual entheogen?
Of the 68 species bearing this name, only the Aquilinae are genetically "true" ones — the rest just qualify as any bird of prey big enough to hunt sizeable vertebrates; what's the common name?
Eagle: Large bird of prey. Eagle is the common name for certain large birds of prey within the family of the Accipitridae.
This branch of biology and medicine studies the glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream, governing everything from growth to mood and metabolism — what is it called?
Endocrinology: Branch of medicine pertaining to the endocrine system.
Commonly called spurge, this giant plant genus includes the popular Christmas poinsettia and a thorny succulent nicknamed 'crown of thorns' — which genus is it?
A founder of modern topology who also wrote under the playful pen name "Paul Mongré," this German mathematician — Jewish and facing deportation — died by suicide with his family in 1942. Who was he?
Felix Hausdorff: German mathematician (1868–1942). Hausdorff was Jewish, and life became difficult for him and his family after the Kristallnacht of 1938.
Home to the radius and ulna joined by the interosseous membrane, this region of the arm lies between the elbow and the wrist — what is it?
Forearm: Region of the upper limb between the elbow and the wrist.
Naming his most famous pistol after his 17th patent — not for holding seventeen rounds, as many assume — this Austrian engineer got his design into Austrian service in 1982 — who was he?
Prince Carl Philip, Duke of Värmland

The only Allied jet aircraft to see combat in World War II, this British fighter entered service with No. 616 Squadron RAF in July 1944, powered by engines pioneered by Frank Whittle — which aircraft?
Gloster Meteor: Britain's first jet fighter, 1943–1980s.
This motorsport engineer led the Haas Formula One team from 2016 to 2023 before becoming CEO of a MotoGP outfit — who is he?
Guenther Steiner: Italian and American motor racing engineer (born 1965)
Despite common nicknames like 'Christmas rose' and 'Lenten rose,' this poisonous Eurasian flowering genus isn't actually related to roses at all — what is it?
Discovered in 2013 in South Africa's Rising Star Cave system, this small-brained archaic human species yielded over 1,500 bone specimens from at least 15 individuals — which species?
Homo naledi: South African archaic human species. The initial discovery comprises 1,550 specimens of bone, representing 737 different skeletal elements, and at least 15 different individuals.

Diagnosed via Whipple's triad and most often triggered by diabetes medications like insulin, this condition causes shakiness, confusion, and sweating when blood sugar drops below 70 mg/dL — what is it?

Hypoglycemia: Decrease in blood sugar. It is defined as blood glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L), symptoms associated with hypoglycemia, and resolution of symptoms when blood sugar returns to normal.
Most often extracted from chicory, this plant-stored fructan earned FDA approval as a dietary fiber in 2018 and remains the gold-standard compound for measuring kidney filtration rates — what is it?
A Communist Party member and Stanford-trained psychiatrist, this woman is best remembered for her romantic relationship with J. Robert Oppenheimer, which put her under FBI surveillance. Who is she?
Personal physician to the Buddha and King Bimbisāra in 5th-century BCE Rājagṛha, this 'Medicine King' is still revered by traditional healers across Asia — who is he?

Jīvaka: Personal physician of the Buddha and Indian King Bimbisara. Jīvaka (Pali: Jīvaka Komārabhacca; Sanskrit: Jīvaka Kaumārabhṛtya) was the personal physician (Sanskrit: vaidya) of the Buddha and the Indian King Bimbisāra.
These paired skin folds run from the mons pubis to the perineum and are considered the anatomical counterpart to the male scrotum — what are they called?
Labia majora: Folds of skin that contain and protect the vulva's other parts.

Elon Musk's praise for his MIT driver-attention study on Tesla's autopilot brought this computer scientist to prominence in 2019, ahead of a career hosting long-form interviews with notable figures — who is he?
Lex Fridman: American scientist and podcast host (born 1983)
Sold as Ativan, this benzodiazepine treats anxiety, insomnia, and active seizures, and is even used during surgery to interfere with memory formation — what medication is it?
Lorazepam: Benzodiazepine medication. Lorazepam, sold under the brand name Ativan among others, is a benzodiazepine medication.
This genus of some 32 to 57 deciduous tree and shrub species in the rose family includes the domesticated orchard fruit tree along with crab and wild varieties — what genus is it?
Malus: Flowering genus, rose family Rosaceae.
Originally designated the DC-9 Series 80, this five-abreast single-aisle airliner first flew in October 1979 and entered service with launch customer Swissair the following year — what jet is it?
McDonnell Douglas MD-80: Jet airliner model, series based on the DC-9.

This American climatologist pioneered techniques to pull climate signals from noisy data, building a famous reconstruction of the past thousand years' temperatures with two co-authors in 1998 — who is he?
Michael E. Mann: American physicist and climatologist. Michael Evan Mann (born 1965) is an American climatologist and geophysicist.
Born in Taiwan but naturalized in Japan, this businessman invented the world's first prepackaged instant noodle brand and later created Cup Noodles — who is he?
Momofuku Ando: Taiwanese-Japanese inventor and businessman (1910–2007)
Most often triggered by a viral infection and capable of progressing to heart failure or cardiac arrest, which condition involves inflammation of the heart muscle itself?

Myocarditis: Inflammation of the heart muscle. Myocarditis can progress to inflammatory cardiomyopathy when there is associated ventricular remodeling and cardiac dysfunction due to chronic inflammation.
This Danish physicist won the 1922 Nobel Prize for a model of the atom in which electrons leap between discrete, stable orbits around the nucleus — who is he?
Native to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, this striped mammal looks like a zebra crossbred with a giraffe but is actually the giraffe's closest living relative — which animal?
Okapi: Species of mammal. Although the okapi has striped markings reminiscent of zebras, it is most closely related to the giraffe.
A reactive nonmetal of the chalcogen group, it's the most abundant element in Earth's crust — locked into water, silicates, and rust — and the third-most abundant in the universe. What is it?
Oxygen: Chemical element with atomic number 8 (O)
Carl Linnaeus named this crop 'hypogaea' — Greek for 'under the earth' — because, unlike most legumes, it ripens its pods below ground. What is it?
Peanut: Legume cultivated as a grain and oil crop.
This anxiety disorder involves an irrational, excessive fear that persists more than six months and can trigger fainting in blood-or-injury cases — what is it?
Phobia: Anxiety disorder classified by a persistent and excessive fear of an object or situation.
First synthesized in 1940 by bombarding uranium-238 with deuterons at UC Berkeley, this radioactive metal can expand up to 70% in volume when its surface oxidizes — which element?
Plutonium: Chemical element with atomic number 94 (Pu)
Discovered in 1857 by French chemist Marcellin Berthelot, this three-carbon alkane turns liquid under pressure and now fuels countless backyard barbecues — what gas is it?
A group of these mid-sized Galliformes birds is called a covey or bevy, and 40 million of them were farm-raised in the US back in 2007 alone — what bird is it?
Quail: Index of animals with the same common name.
Found in grape skins and produced by plants as a defense against injury or infection, this compound is touted as a longevity supplement despite scant evidence it helps — what is it?
Resveratrol: Polyphenol with a stilbene skeleton.
Operating under the alias 'Dread Pirate Roberts,' this American created and ran the dark-web marketplace Silk Road until his 2013 FBI arrest — who is he?
Ross Ulbricht: American cybercriminal founder of Silk Road (born 1984)

Sometimes nicknamed the "seven-year itch," this contagious infestation by a tiny burrowing mite spreads fastest in crowded places and announces itself with fierce itching and a pimple-like rash — what is it?
Nicknamed the 'Human Computer' for her lightning mental arithmetic, this Indian writer also authored one of the earliest studies of homosexuality in India, back in 1977 — who is she?
Shakuntala Devi: Indian writer and mental calculator (1929–2013)
Known commonly as chlorine bleach when dissolved in water, this unstable inorganic compound decomposes to release chlorine gas — what is it?
Sodium hypochlorite: Chemical compound. Sodium hypochlorite is an alkaline inorganic chemical compound with the formula NaOCl (also written as NaClO).
Famous for kite-shaped plates along its back and spikes on its tail, this Late Jurassic herbivore may have been preyed on by Allosaurus — which dinosaur?
Stegosaurus: Genus of Late Jurassic armored dinosaur.

Allowing one neuron to send signals to a neighboring cell, this junction can be chemical or electrical, with coupled electrical types creating synchronized brain activity via gap junctions — what is it?
Synapse: Structure connecting neurons in the nervous system.
Patented in 1953 and originally derived from Streptomyces bacteria, this antibiotic treats ailments from acne to cholera to plague by blocking bacterial protein production — which drug?
Tetracycline: Antibiotic. It is available in oral and topical formulations.
Home to more than 4,200 described species, this family of large crane flies can be identified by the length of their maxillary palps — what is it?
Tipulidae: Family of flies. There are more than 30 genera and 4,200 described species in Tipulidae, common and widespread throughout the world.
Also called the jigger or chigoe flea, this burrowing parasite causes an infestation known as tungiasis and is often mistaken for an unrelated mite — which species?
Tunga penetrans: Species of flea. It is a parasitic insect found in most tropical and sub-tropical climates.
Caused by white blood cells migrating into and damaging vessel walls, this group of disorders inflames both arteries and veins, and sometimes even the lymphatic vessels — what condition is it?
Vasculitis: Medical disorders that destroy blood vessels by inflammation.
With a heart-shaped white facial disc and an eerie screech instead of a hoot, this nocturnal hunter locates small mammals purely by sound — which bird?
Western barn owl: Species of owl. The western barn owl (Tyto alba) is a species of barn owl native to Europe, southwestern Asia, and Africa.
Nicknamed the ZZ plant or eternity plant, this glossy-leaved houseplant genus native to eastern Africa is prized for being nearly impossible to kill — name the genus?
Zamioculcas: Species of plant. Zamioculcas is a genus of flowering plants in the family Araceae, containing the single species Zamioculcas zamiifolia.
Xenon is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for xenon is Xe. Xenon is a chemical element; it has symbol Xe and atomic number 54.
Bismuth is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for bismuth is Bi. Bismuth is a chemical element; it has symbol Bi and atomic number 83.
